node.title: ATP use in active transport
node.canonical_question: How do cells use ATP to power active transport across membranes?
node.summary: Membrane pumps like the sodium-potassium ATPase hydrolyse ATP to move ions against their concentration gradient.

render.heading: How cells use ATP for active transport
render.body:
ATP is the cell's main energy currency, and one of its most important jobs is powering active transport — the movement of molecules across a membrane against their concentration gradient (that is, from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration).

Passive transport moves molecules down their gradient and requires no energy. Active transport does the opposite, so it needs an energy input. That energy comes from ATP.

How it works:

1. A membrane protein called a pump spans the cell membrane. A well-known example is the sodium-potassium pump (Na+/K+ ATPase), found in nearly every animal cell.

2. The pump binds a molecule of ATP. An enzyme domain on the pump hydrolyses (breaks) the ATP into ADP and inorganic phosphate, releasing energy.

3. This energy causes the pump to change shape. The shape change moves specific ions from one side of the membrane to the other, against their gradient.

4. For the sodium-potassium pump specifically, each cycle moves three sodium ions (Na+) out of the cell and two potassium ions (K+) into the cell, maintaining the ion balance that nerve and muscle cells depend on.

Why this matters:

Active transport keeps concentration gradients across cell membranes from collapsing. These gradients are essential for nerve signalling, muscle contraction, nutrient uptake, and many other processes. Because maintaining these gradients costs energy, cells must continuously produce ATP — which is why cellular respiration is so important.
